articles.title: With turbulence all around, Armani plays it safe and easy in Milan
articles.summary: The late designer’s niece echoes his sense of relaxation, as the house seeks to prove itself to potential buyers. A year after the death of Giorgio Armani, the Italian fashion house he founded in 1975 is facing increasing uncertainty about its future ownership.
body: In his will, Armani, who ruled over the business for 50 years, instructed his heirs to sell an initial 15% stake of the company within 18 months of his death. If a private sale does not materialise, an IPO is mandated to take place. Now there are reports the group is readying itself for formal talks with the French conglomerate LVMH, the beauty giant L’Oréal and the eyewear group EssilorLuxottica – three of Armani’s preferred acquirers – over the possible sale of a minority stake.

Against this backdrop, pressure is mounting for the company to prove to potential buyers the continued allure of Armani. In 2025, its revenue fell for a second consecutive year, dropping 2.8% to €2.19bn.
In a turbulent luxury market, the question now is if Armani can remain a powerhouse without its founder – who turned it into an empire – at the helm.

So far during this era of upheaval, Armani’s niece Silvana Armani, who took over as creative director of womenswear after his death, has chosen to play it safe by leaning into continuity rather than any dramatic design shake-up.
points: The late designer’s niece echoes his sense of relaxation, as the house seeks to prove itself to potential buyers.
A year after the death of Giorgio Armani, the Italian fashion house he founded in 1975 is facing increasing uncertainty about its future ownership.

articles.title: When a celebrity dies, it can feel like losing a loved one. Why do we get so invested in parasocial relationships? | Bianca Denny
articles.summary: These one-sided connections with famous people are a normal part of modern life. But sometimes they can lead to emotional distress. The modern mind is a column where experts discuss mental health issues they are seeing in their work. “It came as such a shock.
body: Psychologists are accustomed to seeing bereaved individuals. But working with Jodie* presented a unique challenge – she’d never met the person she was grieving. Jodie was reeling after the recent death of a well known singer. Despite not knowing the singer personally, Jodie’s grief and loss seemed as palpable as other patients speaking about the deaths of family members or loved ones. Jodie reported that weeks after the singer’s death, she was struggling to attend work and was sleeping poorly, describing herself as consumed with thoughts of the singer.

Jodie was experiencing grief related to a parasocial relationship. This is a social phenomenon in which a person experiences a one-sided psychological connection with a public figure or famous person. While an intimate and intense sense of friendship or connection is felt, the object of attention is oblivious to their admirer’s existence.
points: These one-sided connections with famous people are a normal part of modern life.
But sometimes they can lead to emotional distress.
The modern mind is a column where experts discuss mental health issues they are seeing in their work.

articles.title: The kindness of strangers: Two helicopter pilots flew down low to wave to my three-year-old son – he was beside himself with joy
articles.summary: My son adores helicopters, so we waved as hard as possible as it flew past. Then it suddenly looped and came back around. My sister lives in Ukraine; I live in Australia. We had gone five long years without seeing each other when we finally reunited during a trip to Los Angeles.
body: We had a lot of conversations about people and kindness that day. I told her how I had noticed a softer side to men since having a son. As a woman, you’re often wary of construction workers, for example – what might they say to me when I walk past? But now when I pass a building site with my son, the workers often let him play with their radio, or beep a tractor to make him laugh. It was very heartwarming and gave me a whole new perspective on the other sex.
As I shared this observation with my sister, a coastguard helicopter flew overhead. My son adores helicopters and is always fascinated to see one, so we all waved as hard as possible as it flew past.

But instead of carrying on up the coast, the helicopter suddenly looped and came back around. It began flying super low and circled around us twice, with both pilots – two men – waving at my son and mouthing “Hi!” from the cockpit. It was so close it felt like it almost landed right in front of us.
We were shocked, as was everyone else at the beach – many people began filming. My sister burst into tears. My son was beside himself with joy. It was, simply, the coolest thing ever.
points: My son adores helicopters, so we waved as hard as possible as it flew past.
Then it suddenly looped and came back around.
My sister lives in Ukraine; I live in Australia.
We had a lot of conversations about people and kindness that day.

articles.title: Lime bike profits double as rider numbers surge in England
articles.summary: US-owned firm says average monthly users at its UK arm surged to 700,000 with sales up by a third. Love them or hate them, Lime ebikes are an increasingly common sight on England’s roads with new figures showing annual profits more than doubling thanks to a surge in riders.
body: Lime’s average number of monthly users jumped 31% to approaching 700,000 as it added more than 4,500 ebikes and scooters to its fleet, taking the total to almost 38,000, the company’s UK arm, Lime Technologies, said in accounts filed at Companies House.

Sales rose by a third to £148m in 2025 and profits more than doubled to £4.7m from £1.7m, as first reported by the Sunday Times. The progress followed expansion into new cities, including Oxford in 2024 and Nottingham in 2023, adding to its presence in London, Milton Keynes and Salford.

Despite the surge in trade, Lime’s UK accounts show it employed just 54 people in 2025, up from 39 a year before, largely because it relies on self-employed contractors to shift and service its ebikes and scooters.

The company, whose parent, Neutron Holdings, listed on the Nasdaq stock exchange last year valued at $1.7bn (£1.3bn), is part-owned by US ride-hailing app Uber. Lime was founded in 2017 in San Francisco, California, and now operates in about 230 cities across 29 countries, mostly in Europe.

articles.title: Gianvito Rossi Marked 20 Years of Fabulous Footwear and a New Rizzoli Tome
articles.summary: For the brand’s 20th anniversary celebration at Palazzo Serbelloni during Milan Fashion Week, both Naomi Watts and Paloma Elsesser turned up in the Jessica—and told Vogue they were more than happy to spend the evening on their feet.
body: “I love the comfort and elegance,” said Watts, who styled her Jessicas with an Attersee pleated halter top and wide-leg trousers. “For me, elegance quickly fades if it’s not comfortable. Some people will suffer, but I don’t want to anymore.”

Elsesser, who also selected plexi Gianvito Rossis for her Vogue fall shopping guide, teamed her pair with a vintage Jean Paul Gaultier skirt and a leather bustier she thrifted in Paris. “There’s an admiration and a thought of the sensuality of women, but the need for comfort as well,” she said.

Rossi is deeply inspired by Umberto Boccioni’s Unique Forms of Continuity in Space, the Futurist sculpture of a figure striding forward, its body fragmented into aerodynamic forms that suggest speed and movement. The designer told Vogue that there are “two souls” to every collection, or perhaps that should be soles: one rooted in the house’s design language and another devoted to inventing new ideas that might eventually become signatures themselves. “There’s a part of the collection that is more about evolution, and there’s another part of the collection that is more about innovation,” he said.

articles.title: Cashmere Headphones and a Punk Rock Performance: Inside Thom Browne and Bose’s Bash at The Lotos Club
articles.summary: Thom Browne celebrated his Bose launch with an experiential event in the Upper East Side gilded age mansion, featuring a performance by Danish group Iceage.
body: Early fans of Thom Browne may recall his first-ever runway show in 2005. It saw two indie rock groups, competing in a haute take on a “battle of the bands” on the third floor of Bergdorf Goodman’s menswear store. Thursday night’s scene at the Lotos Club on Manhattan’s Upper East Side, celebrating the arrival of the label’s collaboration with Bose, had airs of the same scene, but felt more akin to a house party in a gilded home while the parents were out of town.

The members clubhouse for famed thespians and bookish types like Angela Lansbury, Solomon R. Guggenheim, and Tom Wolfe dates back to 1870 and opened in its current location in 1947, just a few feet away from Central Park. Usually the site of lectures and literary discussions, on this occasion it saw a full immersion into the Thom Browne universe and ended with an altogether unexpected performance.
points: Thom Browne celebrated his Bose launch with an experiential event in the Upper East Side gilded age mansion, featuring a performance by Danish group Iceage.

articles.title: From the Archives: Revisiting the Inception of Isaac Mizrahi’s Documentary, Unzipped
articles.summary: Unzipped, a delightful documentary about the life and times of Isaac Mizrahi, tells you everything you ever wanted to know about the fashion industry—and then some.
body: “Zippity-do-da,” by Charles Gandee, was originally published in the September 1995 issue of Vogue.

But what’s truly beyond the pale of even the most fecund imagination is the notion that any one of these high-profile designers would risk his public persona by inviting a film crew along to capture him indulging in the kind of shenanigans that tend to get a guy noticed in a way that most guys would prefer not to get noticed.

In the fraternity of American fashion designers, Isaac Mizrahi is one of a kind. He’s funny and flamboyant, smart and sassy, nervy and, as he will be the first to say, “nelly.” Mizrahi has not only the chutzpah to reveal the rainbow that is his personality but the panache to revel in its many splendid colors—not all of which are flattering. It is precisely this take-me-as-I-am—or don’t—quality that makes Unzipped, the 73-minute documentary about a year in the life of the 33-year-old designer, such a joy.
And if there is one thing sorely missing from the contemporary, which is to say post-Funny Face, crop of films focused on the fashion industry, then that one thing is joy.
points: Unzipped, a delightful documentary about the life and times of Isaac Mizrahi, tells you everything you ever wanted to know about the fashion industry—and then some.

articles.title: Exclusive: Gucci Got the Gang Together for a Late Night After-Party
articles.summary: Hours after presenting his Spring 2027 show, Demna gathered his crew from the front row and runway for an intimate dinner that began in the courtyard of Il Bolognese over Negronis.
body: There are few things more Milanese on a Friday night than a chic, late dinner at restaurant Il Bolognese. This past Friday, though, the crowd wasn’t the usual local mix.

Camila Morrone arrived wearing a black dress and a huge white faux fur while Lindsey Vonn wore a black leather jacket with monogrammed pumps and a matching Horsebit bag. Photographer Jacques Burga moved through the space with his camera, catching everyone before they made their way into the wood-paneled restaurant.

That was when the extent of the eclectic guest list really came into focus. Keke Palmer and Anok Yai joined Bianca Jagger at her table; Nadia Lee Cohen sat with Manu Ríos. Around the room, Aryna Sabalenka—fresh from the US Open—joined Naomi Watts, Yahya Abdul-Mateen II, Romeo Beckham, Alton Mason, Bloody Osiris, and YT.

articles.title: How to Get Empire State Building Tickets for Your Next Trip to NYC
articles.summary: Everything you need to know before visiting New York City’s most iconic skyscraper.
body: Ready to experience the Art Deco masterpiece yourself? Read on for everything you need to know before visiting the Empire State Building, including how to get tickets, what’s worth it, the best times to visit, and insider tips for how to make the most of your tourist dollars.

The Empire State Building is a 102-story Art Deco skyscraper located in Midtown Manhattan, designed by Shreve, Lamb & Harmon, and constructed swiftly between the years of 1930 and 1931 (that’s about 4.5 stories per week, making it one of the fastest large-scale construction projects in history). Standing at 1,454 feet tall, it held the title of the world’s tallest building for almost 40 years—that is, until the North Tower of the World Trade Center kicked it down the list in 1970. Today, it’s the eighth tallest building in New York City, and houses over 150 offices, most notably companies like LinkedIn, Workday, and Expedia.
points: Everything you need to know before visiting New York City’s most iconic skyscraper.
